title: BGP Extended Communities Attribute
summary: Defines the extended community attribute for BGP-4, a mechanism for labeling information carried in BGP. The labels can control how routing information is distributed or serve other applications. It is standards-track and was later updated by RFC 7153 and RFC 7606.

plainLanguage.summary: BGP Extended Communities attach structured labels to routes. The type field tells routers what each label means and whether it should travel across an Autonomous System boundary.

subtitle: A structured eight-octet BGP label for identifying and handling routes.

tldr.problem: The original BGP Communities attribute has a limited range and no internal structure for grouping labels by purpose.
tldr.mechanism: The Extended Communities attribute carries 8-octet values with a type field that describes the value layout and whether it is transitive across AS boundaries.
tldr.outcome: The attribute supports structured route labels such as Route Target and Route Origin. RFC 4360 has been updated by RFC 7153 and RFC 7606.

today: RFC 4360 is a Proposed Standard and has been updated by RFC 7153 and RFC 7606.

sections.title: Why BGP Communities Were Extended
sections.content:
The Extended Community Attribute labels information carried in BGP-4. The labels can influence how routing information is distributed or support other applications. Compared with the earlier Communities attribute, extended communities provide a larger range and a Type field that structures the value space.

That structure lets policy select communities by type, rather than listing every individual value. It also indicates whether a community is transitive across an Autonomous System (AS) boundary.
sections.plainLanguage: Extended communities label routes with values that have defined types. Routers can apply policy to a type of label instead of listing every value separately.

sections.title: The Eight-Octet Attribute
sections.content:
The Extended Communities Attribute is a transitive optional BGP attribute with Type Code 16. It contains a set of extended communities, each exactly 8 octets. Each value has a Type field of 1 or 2 octets and a Value field containing the remaining octets.

The high-order Type octet includes an IANA authority bit and a transitivity bit. A transitive community can cross AS boundaries; a non-transitive community should be removed before a route is advertised across an AS boundary. Two communities are equal only if all 8 octets match.
sections.plainLanguage: Each extended community is eight bytes long. Its type identifies the value's format and whether it can cross network boundaries.

sections.title: Three Value Layouts
sections.content:
The RFC defines three templates for extended values. A Two-Octet AS Specific value contains a 2-octet AS number and a 4-octet local value. An IPv4 Address Specific value contains a 4-octet IPv4 address and a 2-octet local value. An Opaque value contains a 6-octet value interpreted according to its sub-type.

Each template has a 2-octet Type field and a 6-octet Value field. The sub-type identifies the particular kind of community within the template.
sections.plainLanguage: The type selects one of three layouts for the value. The layouts reserve space for an AS number, an IPv4 address, or a value defined by a sub-type.

sections.title: Route Target and Route Origin
sections.content:
A Route Target identifies routers that may receive routes carrying the community. Its sub-type is 0x02. A Route Origin identifies routers that inject routes into BGP, and its sub-type is 0x03. Both are transitive across an AS boundary.

For each community, the Global Administrator field can contain an AS number or an IPv4 address, depending on the template. RFC 4364 describes one possible use for these communities.
sections.plainLanguage: A Route Target identifies where a route may be distributed. A Route Origin identifies where a route entered BGP.

sections.title: How BGP Speakers Handle Communities
sections.content:
A BGP speaker may use extended communities to control which routing information it accepts or advertises. It MUST NOT use them to alter best-path selection in a way that creates forwarding loops. A speaker may add the attribute to a route or modify its values according to local policy.

By default, when routes are aggregated and the resulting attributes do not carry ATOMIC_AGGREGATE, the aggregate should include the union of the communities on the input routes. Local configuration may override this behavior.
sections.plainLanguage: Routers can read, add, or change extended communities according to local policy. Route aggregation normally keeps the communities from the routes being combined.

sections.title: Type Registries and Allocation
sections.content:
IANA maintains a registry for BGP Extended Communities Types. Regular types use an 8-bit value and extended types use a 16-bit value. A value allocated for one class must not be reused in the other class in a conflicting position.

Type assignments specify whether a community is transitive. The RFC defines allocation ranges for Standards Action, Early IANA Allocation, First Come First Served, and experimental use. It also creates registries for the Two-octet AS Specific, IPv4 Address Specific, and Opaque classes.
sections.plainLanguage: IANA maintains the official list of community types. Separate ranges and assignment rules help prevent two types from using the same value.
